einzeiler: Helping middle and high school students with ADHD navigate time blindness and…
kurzfassung: Dr. Suzanne Allen explores the concept of time blindness in teens and tweens with ADHD and its impact on daily life. She shares practical strategies for parents to redesign thinking, communication, and environments to support their children. The session also addresses audience questions on managing morning routines, avoiding micromanagement, and handling failed organizational tools.
stichpunkte: Time blindness affects both how teens experience time and how they use it to plan their days.
Temporal myopia causes young people with ADHD to struggle with deadlines that are far in the future.
Adolescent developmental changes and longer time horizons increase the friction around time management during middle and high school.
Understanding and compassion are essential clinical components of intervention that help protect the parent-teen relationship.
Time blindness manifests in four modes: lateness, panic, messy transitions, and waiting mode.
Redesigning thinking involves recognizing that missed deadlines reflect time blindness rather than a lack of motivation.
Improving communication relies on validation, curious and non-judgmental language, and alternative low-verbal formats.
Environmental redesigns make time visible through clocks, color coding, LED lights, and auditory cues like playlists.
Practical execution strategies include building buffer time, creating runways, and utilizing body doubling.

kapitel.titel: The Impact on Adolescents and Four Modes of Time Blindness
Strategies for Working with Time Differently
Q&A: Morning Routines, Micromanagement, and Tools

clips.hook: The same 20 minutes can feel completely different
clips.text: The exact same duration of time feels fast during enjoyable activities and painfully slow during boring tasks.

clips.hook: Temporal myopia makes distant deadlines blurry
clips.text: Upcoming tasks look hazy when they are far away, failing to generate the necessary energy until they arrive abruptly.

clips.hook: When struggles are invisible, people assume the worst
clips.text: Observers tend to invent negative explanations like laziness or disrespect when a difficulty cannot be physically seen.

clips.hook: What time is the button seat time?
clips.text: A humorous family phrase prompts people to account for minor delays like finding shoes rather than just departure time.

clips.hook: Do not pick seventeen strategies at once
clips.text: Attempting too many changes simultaneously sets unrealistic expectations and overcomplicates the process.

beschreibung:
Suzanne Allen, Psy.D., discusses the four time-blindness modes and what they look like in daily life; how time blindness can affect academics, relationships, and sense of self; how to respond in supportive ways; and about strategies to support stronger time awareness.
